objective: In-text citations include author's last name and year.；Parenthetical citations place author and year in parentheses at end of sentence before period.；Narrative citations integrate author name into sentence, followed by year in parentheses.

learningGoals.statement: Differentiate between parenthetical and narrative in-text citations and apply rules for multiple authors, unknown author, and missing publication year.
Format short and long quotations correctly, including indicating changes with ellipsis, brackets, and [sic].
Paraphrase effectively while providing proper in-text citation.

knowledgeNodes.name: In-Text Citation
knowledgeNodes.definition: In-text citations are used to credit sources within the text, typically including author's last name and year. They come in parenthetical (author and year in parentheses at end of sentence) and narrative (author name in sentence) forms. Special rules apply for multiple authors (use 'et al.' for three or more), unknown author (use organization name or title), and no publication year (use 'n.d.').
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the use of appropriate communication techniques related to business management.

knowledgeNodes.name: Quotation
knowledgeNodes.definition: Quotations must be exactly as original, enclosed in quotation marks for short quotes (<40 words) or set as indented block for long quotes (≥40 words). Changes can be indicated with ellipsis for omissions, square brackets for insertions, or '[sic]' for errors. Quotes must be cited with author, year, and page number.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.

knowledgeNodes.name: Paraphrasing
knowledgeNodes.definition: Paraphrasing is restating a passage in your own words while preserving meaning. Steps include reading, noting key concepts, writing without looking, comparing, and citing. Tips include starting at a different point, using synonyms, changing sentence structure, and breaking or combining sentences.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.

knowledgeNodes.name: References
knowledgeNodes.definition: A reference contains author, date, title, and source. References can be created manually or using tools like Scribbr (by entering source details) or Google Scholar (by copying the APA citation).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct parenthetical citation for a book by Smith (2020)?

options.label: A
options.text: Smith (2020) argues that management is key.
options.feedbackWrong: That's a narrative citation. Parenthetical places both author and year in parentheses at the end of the sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Management is key (Smith, 2020).
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Parenthetical citation includes author and year in parentheses before the period.

options.label: C
options.text: Smith, 2020, argues that management is key.
options.feedbackWrong: This format is not APA style. The year should be in parentheses.

options.label: D
options.text: (Smith, 2020) argues that management is key.
options.feedbackWrong: The parentheses should contain both author and year, but the sentence structure is incorrect. The citation should not be part of the subject.

questions.successCriteria: Identifies correct format for parenthetical citation.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the use of appropriate communication techniques related to business management.
questions.alignmentNote: In-text citation formatting is a communication technique directly aligned with A2.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding of parenthetical vs narrative citation placement.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think the citation must be part of the sentence subject or misplace the year.

questions.stem: A source has four authors: Lee, Park, Kim, and Chen (2022). The first in-text citation should be:

options.label: A
options.text: (Lee et al., 2022)
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. For three or more authors, use the first author's name followed by 'et al.' from the first citation.

options.label: B
options.text: (Lee, Park, Kim, & Chen, 2022)
options.feedbackWrong: That format is for two authors only. For three or more, use 'et al.' even in the first citation.

options.label: C
options.text: (Lee et al. 2022)
options.feedbackWrong: Missing the comma before the year. APA requires a comma after 'et al.' and the year.

options.label: D
options.text: (Lee, et al., 2022)
options.feedbackWrong: No comma after the author's name before 'et al.' in APA style.

questions.successCriteria: Correctly applies 'et al.' for three or more authors in an in-text citation.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the use of appropriate communication techniques related to business management.
questions.alignmentNote: Applying citation rules is part of appropriate communication techniques.
questions.stemIntent: Check application of 'et al.' rule for multiple authors.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think all authors must be listed in first citation or misuse comma placement.

questions.stem: You are citing a website with no publication date. The correct in-text citation is:

options.label: A
options.text: (Organization, n.d.)
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. When no date, use 'n.d.' for 'no date'.

options.label: B
options.text: (Organization, unknown)
options.feedbackWrong: APA uses 'n.d.' not 'unknown'.

options.label: C
options.text: (Organization)
options.feedbackWrong: You must include a year or 'n.d.'.

options.label: D
options.text: (Organization, 2023)
options.feedbackWrong: There is no date, so you cannot assume a year.

questions.successCriteria: Recalls the correct format for no date: 'n.d.'.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the use of appropriate communication techniques related to business management.
questions.alignmentNote: Knowing the 'n.d.' convention is part of citation technique.
questions.stemIntent: Check recall of the 'n.d.' rule for sources without a date.
questions.commonMisconception: Students either omit the date or use an invented year.

questions.stem: A direct quotation is 45 words long. According to APA, how should it be formatted?

options.label: A
options.text: Enclosed in quotation marks and included in the paragraph.
options.feedbackWrong: Quotes of 40 words or more should be set in a block format without quotation marks.

options.label: B
options.text: Set on a new line, indented from the left margin, and no quotation marks.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Long quotes (40+ words) are block quotes: new line, indented, no quotation marks.

options.label: C
options.text: Enclosed in quotation marks and indented from the left margin.
options.feedbackWrong: Quotation marks are not used for block quotes; they should be plain text.

options.label: D
options.text: Italicized and centred.
options.feedbackWrong: APA does not use italics or centering for block quotes.

questions.successCriteria: Distinguishes between short and long quote formatting rules.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
questions.alignmentNote: Quotation formatting is part of the communication process.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding of the 40-word threshold for block quotes.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think long quotes still need quotation marks or are treated the same as short quotes.

questions.stem: When quoting a source that contains a spelling error, you should:

options.label: A
options.text: Correct the error silently.
options.feedbackWrong: You must not change the original text. Use [sic] to indicate the error is in the original.

options.label: B
options.text: Add '[sic]' after the error.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. '[sic]' indicates the error appears in the original source.

options.label: C
options.text: Omit the error using ellipsis.
options.feedbackWrong: Ellipsis indicates omitted words, not errors. Use [sic] for errors.

options.label: D
options.text: Ignore it; spelling errors are acceptable in quotes.
options.feedbackWrong: Quotes must be exact, but you should still indicate with [sic] that the error is not yours.

questions.successCriteria: Correctly identifies the use of [sic] for errors in original quotes.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
questions.alignmentNote: Using [sic] is part of accurate quotation in communication.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding of [sic] for marking errors in direct quotes.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think they can correct errors or omit them without marking.

questions.stem: After paraphrasing a passage from a source, you must:

options.label: A
options.text: No citation is needed because you used your own words.
options.feedbackWrong: Even when paraphrased, the idea is from the source and must be cited.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide an in-text citation with author and year.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Paraphrased content still requires a citation to credit the original source.

options.label: C
options.text: Only cite if you use more than three words from the original.
options.feedbackWrong: The amount of words doesn't matter; any borrowed idea needs citation.

options.label: D
options.text: List the source in the reference list but do not cite in text.
options.feedbackWrong: Both in-text citation and reference entry are required.

questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that paraphrasing requires an in-text citation.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
questions.alignmentNote: Paraphrasing and citation are key components of communication.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding that paraphrasing still requires citation.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think paraphrasing does not need citation because the wording is changed.

questions.stem:
Original: 'Effective managers communicate clearly with their teams to ensure goals are understood.'
Which of the following is an acceptable paraphrase?

options.label: A
options.text: Effective managers talk clearly to their teams to make sure goals are understood.
options.feedbackWrong: This is too close to the original; only a few words changed. It risks plagiarism.

options.label: B
options.text: Managers who communicate clearly help their teams understand organizational goals.
options.feedbackCorrect: This restructures the sentence and changes wording while preserving meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: Effective managers communicate clearly with their teams.
options.feedbackWrong: This is a shortened version of the original, still too similar.

options.label: D
options.text: Teams understand goals when managers communicate effectively.
options.feedbackWrong: This changes structure but keeps 'communicate effectively', which is still quite close; better options exist.

questions.successCriteria: Evaluates which paraphrase is sufficiently original and not too close to the source.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
questions.alignmentNote: Paraphrasing skill is part of the communication process.
questions.stemIntent: Check ability to distinguish acceptable paraphrasing from patchwriting.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think changing a few words is enough; they need to restructure and use synonyms substantially.

reteachModules.trigger: Student confuses the placement of author and year in parenthetical vs narrative citations.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks the author name can be part of the sentence in a parenthetical citation, or that the year can be placed elsewhere.

miniLesson.explain: In-text citations come in two forms: parenthetical and narrative. Parenthetical citations place both the author's last name and year in parentheses at the end of the sentence, before the period. Narrative citations integrate the author's name into the sentence itself, with the year in parentheses immediately after the author's name.
miniLesson.example: Correct parenthetical: 'Management is key (Smith, 2020).' Correct narrative: 'Smith (2020) argues that management is key.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: N for Name in sentence; P for Parentheses at the end.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which is a correct parenthetical citation?
A. Jones (2019) states that...
B. (Jones, 2019)
C. Jones, 2019, states that...
guidedPractice.answer: B

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following narrative citation as a parenthetical citation: 'Lee (2021) found that team cohesion improves performance.'
guidedPractice.answer: Team cohesion improves performance (Lee, 2021).

guidedPractice.prompt: Correct the citation format: '(Smith, 2020) argues that management is key.'
guidedPractice.answer: Smith (2020) argues that management is key. (or 'Management is key (Smith, 2020).')

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly selects or applies 'et al.' for two authors or fails to use it for three or more authors.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think 'et al.' is used for any number of authors, or that all authors must be listed in the first citation.

miniLesson.explain: In APA style, for sources with three or more authors, use only the first author's name followed by 'et al.' in every in-text citation. Do not use 'et al.' for two authors; instead, list both authors each time.
miniLesson.example: Correct: (Lee et al., 2022) for a source by Lee, Park, Kim, and Chen. Incorrect: (Lee, Park, Kim, & Chen, 2022) for first citation – use 'et al.' from the start.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think: 'Three or more, et al. is the core. Two authors, list them both.'

guidedPractice.prompt: A source has five authors: Johnson, Smith, Brown, Taylor, and Wilson (2021). What is the correct in-text citation?
guidedPractice.answer: (Johnson et al., 2021)

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify the error: In a paper, the student wrote (Davis & Lee, 2019) for a source with three authors. Is this correct? If not, how should it be written?
guidedPractice.answer: No, for three authors use 'et al.': (Davis et al., 2019).

guidedPractice.prompt: You are writing a paragraph about a study by Miller, Garcia, and Rivera (2020). Create a narrative citation and a parenthetical citation for this source.
guidedPractice.answer: Narrative: Miller et al. (2020) found that... Parenthetical: (Miller et al., 2020)

reteachModules.trigger: Student chooses incorrect option for no-date citation in diagnostic question 3, indicating they forgot to use 'n.d.'.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often omit the year or use an invented year when a source has no publication date, instead of using the APA convention 'n.d.' (no date).

miniLesson.explain: In APA style, when a source does not have a publication date, you use 'n.d.' (which stands for 'no date') in place of the year in both parenthetical and narrative citations. This signals to the reader that the source lacks a publication year.
miniLesson.example: For a report by the Ontario Ministry of Education with no date: Parenthetical: (Ontario Ministry of Education, n.d.) Narrative: Ontario Ministry of Education (n.d.) states...

guidedPractice.prompt: What abbreviation does APA use in an in-text citation when a source has no publication year?
guidedPractice.answer: n.d.

guidedPractice.prompt: You are citing a webpage from the World Health Organization that has no publication date. Write the correct parenthetical citation.
guidedPractice.answer: (World Health Organization, n.d.)

guidedPractice.prompt: A student wrote (Statistics Canada, 2023) for a source that has no date. Is this correct? If not, what should it be?
guidedPractice.answer: Incorrect. It should be (Statistics Canada, n.d.) because the source has no publication year.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly formats a long quotation (≥40 words) by using quotation marks or failing to indent it as a block quote.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often treat all quotations the same: they use quotation marks even for long quotes, or they don't realize the 40-word threshold triggers a different format (block quote, no quotation marks, indented).

miniLesson.explain: In APA style, quotations are formatted differently based on length. Short quotations (fewer than 40 words) are enclosed in double quotation marks and included within the text. Long quotations (40 words or more) are set apart as block quotes: they start on a new line, are indented from the left margin, and do not have quotation marks. The in-text citation for a block quote goes after the final punctuation.
miniLesson.example:
Short quote (<40 words): According to Smith (2020), "Effective management requires clear communication" (p. 45).

Long quote (≥40 words): Smith (2020) found that:

    Management is a complex process that involves planning, organizing, leading, and controlling. Effective managers must adapt their style to the situation and the people they work with. Communication is the key to successful management.

(p. 46)
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: 40 words is the dividing line. Under 40: quote marks. 40 or more: block it (no quotes, indented).

guidedPractice.prompt: Decide if the following quotation is short or long: "The business environment is constantly changing, and managers must be able to adapt to new challenges and opportunities" (15 words).
guidedPractice.answer: Short (under 40 words).

guidedPractice.prompt: Format the following 50-word quotation correctly: "In today's global economy, companies must innovate to stay competitive. Innovation requires a culture that encourages creativity and risk-taking. Managers play a crucial role in fostering such an environment."
guidedPractice.answer: It should be a block quote: new line, indented, no quotation marks, with citation after the period.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student wrote: "Smith (2020) stated that "Management is about achieving goals through people. It involves coordination and motivation of team members to accomplish objectives." This is a 30-word quote." What is wrong? Correct it.
guidedPractice.answer: The quotation is short (<40 words), so it should be enclosed in quotation marks and kept in the paragraph. The student used block format incorrectly. Correct format: Smith (2020) stated that "Management is about achieving goals through people. It involves coordination and motivation of team members to accomplish objectives" (p. 30).

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on question 5 (boh4m-diag-apa-q5)
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think they can correct errors in a quotation or omit them without marking, rather than using '[sic]' to indicate the error is in the original.

miniLesson.explain: When you quote a source directly, you must reproduce it exactly as written, including any errors. To show that the error is in the original and not your own mistake, place the Latin term '[sic]' (meaning 'thus') immediately after the error in square brackets.
miniLesson.example: Original: 'The managment team held a meeting.' → 'The managment [sic] team held a meeting.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think: '[sic] = 'I saw it in the original'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Does the following quotation need '[sic]'? Original: 'The company expereinced growth.' Your quote: 'The company experienced growth.'
guidedPractice.answer: No. The original has a typo 'expereinced', but you corrected it. You must use [sic] if you keep the error. If you correct silently, you are misrepresenting the source. For this quote, you should have used: 'The company expereinced [sic] growth.'

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following direct quotation correctly, adding '[sic]' where needed: Original: 'Their are three departments.' Your quote: 'Their are three departments.'
guidedPractice.answer: 'Their [sic] are three departments.' (The error 'Their' is incorrect; it should be 'There'. [sic] indicates the error is in the original.)

guidedPractice.prompt: You are quoting a sentence: 'The CEO gave a speech about the companies future.' The original has an error ('companies' should be 'company's'). How would you quote it correctly? Would you use [sic], ellipsis, or brackets? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: Use [sic]: 'The CEO gave a speech about the companies [sic] future.' Because the error is a missing apostrophe (possessive), you use [sic] to show it's in the original. Ellipsis is for omissions, and brackets are for insertions or edits for clarity (e.g., adding 'the').

reteachModules.trigger: The student failed to provide an in-text citation when paraphrasing a source.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Many students believe that because paraphrasing uses their own words, they do not need to cite the source. However, the ideas still belong to the original author and must be credited.

miniLesson.explain: Paraphrasing means restating a passage in your own words while keeping the original meaning. Even though you change the wording, you still need to cite the source using an in-text citation (author, year).
miniLesson.example: Original from Roose & Kang (2018): 'Technology executives faced tough questions during the hearings.' Paraphrase: During the hearings, technology executives were asked challenging questions (Roose & Kang, 2018).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: 'Paraphrase but always cite' – like a detective who retells a story but still gives credit to the witness.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: When you paraphrase a source, you do not need to include an in-text citation because the words are your own.
guidedPractice.answer: False. You must always cite the source when paraphrasing.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the following original sentence from Johnson (2021): 'Team collaboration improves project outcomes.' Write a correct paraphrase with an in-text citation.
guidedPractice.answer: According to Johnson (2021), working together as a team leads to better project results.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student wrote: 'Team collaboration enhances project results.' based on Johnson (2021) without citation. Is this acceptable? Explain why and correct the error.
guidedPractice.answer: No, because it lacks an in-text citation. Correct version: 'Team collaboration enhances project results (Johnson, 2021).'

reteachModules.trigger: Student's paraphrased sample is too similar to original wording.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think that changing only a few words or reordering sentences is sufficient for paraphrasing, but they must restructure entirely and use synonyms without looking at the original.

miniLesson.explain: Paraphrasing means restating a passage in your own words without changing the meaning. Simply swapping a few words or altering sentence order while keeping the same structure is called 'patchwriting' and is too close to the original, risking plagiarism. You must fully rewrite the idea using your own language and sentence construction. Steps to paraphrase: read, note key concepts, write without looking, compare, cite. Tips: start at a different point, use synonyms, change sentence structure, break or combine sentences.
miniLesson.example:
Original: 'Effective managers communicate clearly with their teams to ensure goals are understood.'
Too-close: 'Effective managers talk clearly to their teams to make sure goals are understood.'
Good paraphrase: 'Managers who share clear messages help their teams grasp the objectives.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of paraphrasing as retelling a story in your own words – you wouldn't just change 'said' to 'stated'; you'd tell it from a different angle.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Choose the best paraphrase. Original: 'Good leaders listen actively to their employees.'
A) Good leaders listen actively to their workers.
B) Active listening is a key trait of effective leadership.
C) Leaders who listen well are good.
guidedPractice.answer: B) Active listening is a key trait of effective leadership.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite this sentence in your own words: 'The company implemented a new policy to reduce waste.' Provide a paraphrase that is not too close.
guidedPractice.answer: A waste reduction policy was introduced by the firm.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the following passage and write a paraphrase that avoids patchwriting. Passage: 'Teamwork is essential for project success. Each member must contribute their skills and support one another. Effective collaboration leads to better outcomes than individual effort.' Write your paraphrase below.
guidedPractice.answer: Projects thrive when team members combine their abilities and help each other, resulting in superior performance compared to working alone.

questions.rubric: Correct answer integrates the author's name into the sentence, with the year in parentheses immediately after the author name, e.g., 'Kim (2023) states that employee engagement reduces turnover.' or similar wording.

(Chen, Kim, 2021)

(World Health Organization, 2023)

questions.stem: A student wants to quote a passage that is exactly 45 words long. According to APA style, which of the following is the correct way to format it?
options: Enclose the passage in double quotation marks and keep it within the paragraph.
Set the passage as a block quote: start on a new line, indent the entire block, and do not use quotation marks.
Use single quotation marks around the passage and indent it slightly.
Place the passage in italics and include it within the text.

questions.stem: Here is a 52-word quotation from a source: "Effective management requires a combination of technical skills, human skills, and conceptual skills. Technical skills are needed to perform specific tasks, human skills to work with others, and conceptual skills to understand the organization as a whole. These skills are essential at all levels of management." Format this quotation correctly as an APA in-text citation (assume the author is Smith, 2020, page 78). Show exactly how it should appear in the essay, including the citation.
questions.rubric:
Student should format as a block quote: new line, indented from left margin, no quotation marks, citation after the final period. Example: Smith (2020) stated:

    Effective management requires a combination of technical skills, human skills, and conceptual skills. Technical skills are needed to perform specific tasks, human skills to work with others, and conceptual skills to understand the organization as a whole. These skills are essential at all levels of management.

(p. 78)

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: You are writing a paper and want to quote the following sentence from a book: 'The manager said, 'We need to recuit more staff.' ' Which of the following is the correct way to quote this sentence, preserving the original error?
options: "The manager said, 'We need to recuit more staff.'"
"The manager said, 'We need to recuit [sic] more staff.'"
"The manager said, 'We need to recruit more staff.'"
"The manager said, 'We need to recuit ... more staff.'"

questions.stem: The original text reads: 'Their are four main reasons for the decline.' Write the direct quotation as you would include it in your paper, using [sic] to indicate the error.
questions.rubric: The student must write: 'Their [sic] are four main reasons for the decline.' The quote must be identical to the original except that '[sic]' is placed immediately after the error ('Their') in square brackets. Accept variations in quotation mark style (single or double) and punctuation placement, but the word 'Their' must be followed by ' [sic]'.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why you must cite a source when paraphrasing?
options: Because paraphrasing uses some of the original wording.
Because the ideas belong to the original author and must be credited.
Because the citation adds credibility to your writing.
Because the assignment instructions require it.

questions.stem: Original sentence: 'Remote work increases employee productivity (Garcia, 2020).' Write a correct paraphrase of this sentence with an in-text citation.
questions.rubric: Student paraphrases the idea and includes Garcia (2020) or (Garcia, 2020). Example: 'Garcia (2020) found that employees are more productive when working remotely.'

questions.stem: A student wrote: 'Working from home leads to higher productivity.' based on Garcia (2020) but omitted the citation. Explain why this is a problem and correct it.
questions.rubric: Student recognizes that citation is needed because the idea is from Garcia (2020). Correct version includes '(Garcia, 2020)' at the end or 'Garcia (2020) states that...'.

retestCards.passRule: All questions must be answered correctly.

questions.stem: Original: 'Effective managers communicate clearly with their teams to ensure goals are understood.' Which of the following is an acceptable paraphrase (not too close)?
options: Effective managers talk clearly to their teams to make sure goals are understood.
Managers who share clear messages help their teams grasp the objectives.

questions.stem: Rewrite this sentence in your own words without copying the structure or wording too closely: 'Teamwork is essential for project success.'
questions.rubric: The paraphrase must significantly change sentence structure and use synonyms. Accept examples like 'Projects succeed when team members collaborate effectively.' or 'Successful projects rely on team collaboration.' Reject if too similar to original, e.g., 'Teamwork is important for project success.' or 'Teamwork is necessary for project success.'

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly: MCQ selects correct option (1), open-ended response passes rubric check.

dashboardFormat.objective: In-text citations include author's last name and year.；Parenthetical citations place author and year in parentheses at end of sentence before period.；Narrative citations integrate author name into sentence, followed by year in parentheses.

learningGoals.statement: Differentiate between parenthetical and narrative in-text citations and apply rules for multiple authors, unknown author, and missing publication year.
Format short and long quotations correctly, including indicating changes with ellipsis, brackets, and [sic].
Paraphrase effectively while providing proper in-text citation.

nextActions: [err-intext-parenthetical-vs-narrative] student picks wrong option on question 1: You mixed up parenthetical and narrative citation formats. Let's review the difference.
[err-intext-et-al-misuse] student picks wrong option on question 2: You misused 'et al.' Remember: use it for three or more authors, not for two.
[err-intext-nodate-forgotten] student picks wrong option on question 3: You forgot to use 'n.d.' when there's no publication year. Let's practice.
[err-quotation-length-format] student picks wrong option on question 4: Short and long quotes have different formatting rules. Check the 40-word threshold.
[err-quotation-sic-omission] student picks wrong option on question 5: You didn't mark an error in the original quote with [sic]. That's important for accuracy.
[err-paraphrase-no-citation] student answers open-ended without citation or picks wrong option on question 6: Paraphrasing still needs an in-text citation. Always credit the source.
[err-paraphrase-too-close] student's paraphrased sample is too similar to original on question 7: Your paraphrase is too close to the original. Try using synonyms and restructuring sentences.

cards.question: Which of the following is a correct parenthetical citation for a book by Smith (2020)?
options: Smith (2020) argues that management is key.
Management is key (Smith, 2020).
Smith, 2020, argues that management is key.
(Smith, 2020) argues that management is key.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of parenthetical vs narrative citation placement.
misconceptions: That's a narrative citation. Parenthetical places both author and year in parentheses at the end of the sentence.
✓ Correct. Parenthetical citation includes author and year in parentheses before the period.
This format is not APA style. The year should be in parentheses.
The parentheses should contain both author and year, but the sentence structure is incorrect. The citation should not be part of the subject.
cards.successCriteria: Identifies correct format for parenthetical citation.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the use of appropriate communication techniques related to business management.
cards.alignmentNote: In-text citation formatting is a communication technique directly aligned with A2.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think the citation must be part of the sentence subject or misplace the year.

cards.question: A source has four authors: Lee, Park, Kim, and Chen (2022). The first in-text citation should be:
options: (Lee et al., 2022)
(Lee, Park, Kim, & Chen, 2022)
(Lee et al. 2022)
(Lee, et al., 2022)
cards.diagnosis: Check application of 'et al.' rule for multiple authors.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. For three or more authors, use the first author's name followed by 'et al.' from the first citation.
That format is for two authors only. For three or more, use 'et al.' even in the first citation.
Missing the comma before the year. APA requires a comma after 'et al.' and the year.
No comma after the author's name before 'et al.' in APA style.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly applies 'et al.' for three or more authors in an in-text citation.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the use of appropriate communication techniques related to business management.
cards.alignmentNote: Applying citation rules is part of appropriate communication techniques.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think all authors must be listed in first citation or misuse comma placement.

cards.question: You are citing a website with no publication date. The correct in-text citation is:
options: (Organization, n.d.)
(Organization, unknown)
(Organization)
(Organization, 2023)
cards.diagnosis: Check recall of the 'n.d.' rule for sources without a date.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. When no date, use 'n.d.' for 'no date'.
APA uses 'n.d.' not 'unknown'.
You must include a year or 'n.d.'.
There is no date, so you cannot assume a year.
cards.successCriteria: Recalls the correct format for no date: 'n.d.'.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate the use of appropriate communication techniques related to business management.
cards.alignmentNote: Knowing the 'n.d.' convention is part of citation technique.
cards.commonMisconception: Students either omit the date or use an invented year.

cards.question: A direct quotation is 45 words long. According to APA, how should it be formatted?
options: Enclosed in quotation marks and included in the paragraph.
Set on a new line, indented from the left margin, and no quotation marks.
Enclosed in quotation marks and indented from the left margin.
Italicized and centred.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of the 40-word threshold for block quotes.
misconceptions: Quotes of 40 words or more should be set in a block format without quotation marks.
✓ Correct. Long quotes (40+ words) are block quotes: new line, indented, no quotation marks.
Quotation marks are not used for block quotes; they should be plain text.
APA does not use italics or centering for block quotes.
cards.successCriteria: Distinguishes between short and long quote formatting rules.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
cards.alignmentNote: Quotation formatting is part of the communication process.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think long quotes still need quotation marks or are treated the same as short quotes.

cards.question: When quoting a source that contains a spelling error, you should:
options: Correct the error silently.
Add '[sic]' after the error.
Omit the error using ellipsis.
Ignore it; spelling errors are acceptable in quotes.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of [sic] for marking errors in direct quotes.
misconceptions: You must not change the original text. Use [sic] to indicate the error is in the original.
✓ Correct. '[sic]' indicates the error appears in the original source.
Ellipsis indicates omitted words, not errors. Use [sic] for errors.
Quotes must be exact, but you should still indicate with [sic] that the error is not yours.
cards.successCriteria: Correctly identifies the use of [sic] for errors in original quotes.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
cards.alignmentNote: Using [sic] is part of accurate quotation in communication.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think they can correct errors or omit them without marking.

cards.question: After paraphrasing a passage from a source, you must:
options: No citation is needed because you used your own words.
Provide an in-text citation with author and year.
Only cite if you use more than three words from the original.
List the source in the reference list but do not cite in text.
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding that paraphrasing still requires citation.
misconceptions: Even when paraphrased, the idea is from the source and must be cited.
✓ Correct. Paraphrased content still requires a citation to credit the original source.
The amount of words doesn't matter; any borrowed idea needs citation.
Both in-text citation and reference entry are required.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that paraphrasing requires an in-text citation.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
cards.alignmentNote: Paraphrasing and citation are key components of communication.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think paraphrasing does not need citation because the wording is changed.

cards.question:
Original: 'Effective managers communicate clearly with their teams to ensure goals are understood.'
Which of the following is an acceptable paraphrase?
options: Effective managers talk clearly to their teams to make sure goals are understood.
Managers who communicate clearly help their teams understand organizational goals.
Effective managers communicate clearly with their teams.
Teams understand goals when managers communicate effectively.
cards.diagnosis: Check ability to distinguish acceptable paraphrasing from patchwriting.
misconceptions: This is too close to the original; only a few words changed. It risks plagiarism.
✓ This restructures the sentence and changes wording while preserving meaning.
This is a shortened version of the original, still too similar.
This changes structure but keeps 'communicate effectively', which is still quite close; better options exist.
cards.successCriteria: Evaluates which paraphrase is sufficiently original and not too close to the source.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of the communication process within the workplace.
cards.alignmentNote: Paraphrasing skill is part of the communication process.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think changing a few words is enough; they need to restructure and use synonyms substantially.
